sections.title: U'be'alah and Be'ulat Ba'al: What Each Sage Learns from Each Verse
sections.gist: Continuing the question of how Rebbi, Rava and R. Yochanan each derive *kiddushei bi'ah*: two lessons from *u'be'alah*, Rava's *kiddushin ha'mesurin le'vi'ah*, Rebbi's reading of *be'ulat ba'al* tested against the ten-men baraita, and R. Yochanan's double reading.

children.title: Rebbi: U'be'alah Teaches Two Laws
children.gist: Rebbi reads "and he engages in intercourse with her" as teaching both that a woman is betrothed by bi'ah and that a Hebrew maidservant is not acquired that way.

bullets.text: Question: Rebbi uses *u'be'alah* for *kiddushei bi'ah*; where does he learn that a Hebrew maidservant cannot be acquired through bi'ah?

Answer: the verse could simply have said "and he engages in intercourse". The fuller wording "and engages in intercourse with her" teaches two laws: a woman is betrothed by bi'ah, and a Hebrew maidservant is not acquired by it.
The extra letter of *u'be'alah* is what allows one word to carry two *derashot*.

children.title: Rava: Kiddushin Ha'mesurin Le'vi'ah — Arayot or a Self-Made Prohibition?
children.gist: Rava learns from *u'be'alah* that only betrothal that can lead to permitted bi'ah is valid; the shiur sets out Rashi's and Tosafot's readings and the Ran's question from the Kohen Gadol on Yom Kippur.

bullets.text: Rava, as Bar Ahina explained to him: "When a man takes a woman and engages in intercourse with her" teaches that *kiddushin ha'mesurin le'vi'ah* is valid betrothal, and betrothal not given to bi'ah is not.

Question: then where does Rava learn *kiddushei bi'ah*, and that a maidservant is excluded? Answer: the verse could have written "takes a woman or engages in intercourse"; "and engages" teaches all these laws together.
Rashi (on 51a): the principle refers to the *arayot*. Betrothal of a sister or any other *ervah* does not take hold at all.
Tosafot: it is not about *arayot* but about a prohibition of bi'ah created by the betrothal itself, e.g. betrothing one of two sisters without specifying which, so that neither is permitted to him.

The Ran (Ketubot) asks from the opening Mishnah of Yoma: a second wife is prepared for the Kohen Gadol in case his wife dies on Yom Kippur. Could he betroth her on a day when bi'ah is forbidden? A likely answer: the betrothal need only be fit for bi'ah prospectively, and bi'ah is permitted once the day ends.

chart.caption: Two readings of *kiddushin she'ein mesurin le'vi'ah*
rows: Rashi
Betrothal with one of the *arayot*, which never takes hold
A man's own sister
Tosafot
Betrothal that itself creates the prohibition of bi'ah
Betrothing one of two sisters without saying which

children.gist: Rebbi's reading of *be'ulat ba'al* seems contradicted by his own ruling on ten men with a betrothed virgin; R. Zeira shows that ruling rests on "only" (*levado*), not on her losing virgin status.

children.title: Only the Husband Makes Her Be'ulah? The Ten-Men Baraita
children.gist: Rebbi uses *be'ulat ba'al* to teach that only a husband renders her a non-virgin through atypical intercourse, but his ruling on ten men implies another man can too.

bullets.text: Rebbi uses *be'ulat ba'al* (Devarim 22:22) for the law that a husband renders her a non-virgin even through atypical intercourse (*shelo ke'darkah*), but no other man does.
Challenge from a baraita: ten men had intercourse with a *na'arah me'orasah* and she is still a virgin; all are stoned. Rebbi: "I say the first is stoned and the rest strangled."
Inference: for Rebbi, even a man who is not her husband makes her a non-virgin through atypical intercourse.
The baraita speaks of atypical (anal) intercourse, which leaves her physically a virgin; that is why the Tanna kamma stones all ten. *Skilah* is the harsher death penalty than *chenek*.
"*Omer ani*" ("I say") is Rebbi's own locution; acharonim see in it his humility, presenting his view as a personal opinion.

children.title: R. Zeira: All Pay the Fine; Levado Limits Stoning to One
children.gist: Rebbi agrees that all ten pay the fine as for a virgin; stoning goes to the first only because of *levado*, which the Rabbis use for R. Oshaya's and R. Yonatan's baraita.

bullets.text: R. Zeira: Rebbi concedes that all of them pay the fine of a rapist or seducer, as for a virgin.
Why is the death penalty different? "Then the man only [*levado*] who lay with her shall die" (Devarim 22:25): only one man is executed for a virgin.

The Rabbis use *levado* for a baraita. R. Oshaya: "they shall both die" applies only when both are equal; if one cannot be punished (a minor), the other is not executed either. R. Yonatan: *levado* shows that sometimes only one of them is liable.
Rambam (Hilkhot Na'arah Betulah 1) rules the fine is paid only for typical intercourse. The Ra'avad objects that this sugya treats both kinds alike for the fine.

The commentary printed as Tosafot Rid, a defender of the Rambam, explains him: the Torah's offense may be bound up with the change in her status as a virgin, which only a husband's atypical act brings about.

children.title: R. Yochanan: Be'ulat Ba'al, Not Be'ulat Ish — Two Laws
children.gist: R. Yochanan, who learns *kiddushei bi'ah* from *be'ulat ba'al*, also learns from it that only a husband renders her a non-virgin atypically.

bullets.text: Question: R. Yochanan uses *be'ulat ba'al* for *kiddushei bi'ah*; where does he learn that only a husband makes her a non-virgin through atypical intercourse?
Answer: the verse could have said *be'ulat ish* ("with a man"). Saying *be'ulat ba'al* ("with a husband") teaches both: betrothal through bi'ah, and the husband's unique effect.

returns_to.note: The same husband-only law Rebbi drew from this verse

sections.title: Techilat Bi'ah or Sof Bi'ah: When Does Bi'ah Acquire?
sections.gist: Two practical tests, a rival betrothal mid-act and a Kohen Gadol who must marry a virgin, and Ameimar's ruling that the man has *gemar bi'ah* in mind; the shiur brings Tosafot's four reconciliations with Yevamot.

bullets.text: Question: bi'ah has stages. Does its beginning acquire, or its end?

First difference: he began bi'ah, and meanwhile she accepted betrothal from another man. If the start acquires, the other's betrothal is meaningless; if the end acquires, she is betrothed to the other man.
Second difference: a Kohen Gadol acquiring a virgin through bi'ah. If only the end acquires, she is no longer a virgin at the moment of betrothal, so he could not acquire her this way.
Ameimar in the name of Rava: anyone who has intercourse has the completion in mind (*da'ato al gemar bi'ah*), so acquisition comes at the end.
Tension: Yevamot treats the initial penetration (*ha'ara'ah*) as the legally significant act. Tosafot offer four reconciliations (see chart).
Already in the amoraic period *kiddushei bi'ah* was discouraged in practice, but the question of the Kohen Gadol still matters in principle.

sections.title: Bi'ah: Nisu'in at Once, or Only Erusin?
sections.gist: Does bi'ah make her fully married in one act? Three proofs are tested: Abaye's Mishnah on a father's rights, Rava's baraita of the three-year-old, and the exchange between Yochanan ben Bag Bag and R. Yehuda ben Beteira, which turns into a question about *simfon*.

children.title: The Question and Its Tests: Inheritance, Burial Impurity, Vows
children.gist: If bi'ah effects *nisu'in*, the husband inherits her, becomes impure for her burial and annuls her vows alone; if only *erusin*, he does none of these.

bullets.text: Question: does the bi'ah that betroths also effect *nisu'in*, or only *erusin*?
The difference is everything that separates a betrothed woman from a married one: does he inherit her; if he is a kohen, does he become impure to bury her; does he annul her vows without her father?
If bi'ah effects *nisu'in*, he inherits, becomes impure for her and annuls alone. If only *erusin*, he does none of these.
Money and a document effect only the first stage and need chuppah for the second; the question is whether bi'ah skips that two-stage structure.

children.title: Abaye: A Father's Rights, and 'If She Married' — Only Money and Document?
children.gist: The Mishnah in Ketubot lists betrothal by bi'ah and then "if she married", suggesting bi'ah is only *erusin*; the Gemara confines "if she married" to money and document.

bullets.text: Abaye cites the Mishnah (Ketubot 46b): a father controls his daughter's betrothal by money, document or bi'ah; he takes her finds and earnings, annuls her vows, and accepts her *get*; he inherits her but does not eat the produce of her property in her lifetime.
"If she married, the husband has more than he": he eats the produce of her property in her lifetime.
Inference: the Mishnah lists betrothal by bi'ah and then a separate stage of marriage, so bi'ah effects only *erusin*.
Rejection: "if she married" refers to the other modes, money and document, where *erusin* and *nisu'in* are separate. Bi'ah may still effect *nisu'in* at once.

children.title: Rava: The Girl of Three Years and a Day — 'If She Marries a Kohen'
children.gist: A baraita lists the consequences of bi'ah with a girl of three years and a day, then adds "if she marries a kohen"; the Gemara reads that clause as describing the same bi'ah, not a second stage.

bullets.text: Rava cites a baraita: a girl of three years and a day can be betrothed through bi'ah; if her *yavam* has bi'ah with her he acquires her; if she is married, one who has intercourse with her is liable for *eshet ish*.
If she is a *niddah*, she makes the man impure for seven days, and the bedding beneath him becomes impure like the upper one.

If she marries a kohen she eats terumah. If one of the *arayot* has intercourse with her he is executed and she is exempt. If a man of unfit lineage has intercourse with her, he disqualifies her from the priesthood.
Inference: "betrothed through bi'ah" and then "if she marries a kohen" suggest two stages, so bi'ah is not *nisu'in*.
Rejection: the baraita means "if this betrothal through bi'ah is a marriage to a kohen, she eats terumah". One act may be both.
Rashi: below this age the act has no legal standing, "like a finger in the eye". The shiur notes the questions of abuse this raises, which Tosafot already address.
A *niddah*'s bedding becomes a primary source of impurity; the bedding under a man who had relations with her carries only a lesser impurity, like the upper layer above a *zav*.

children.title: Ben Bag Bag and R. Yehuda ben Beteira: May an Arusah Eat Terumah?
children.gist: A third proof: R. Yehuda ben Beteira's *kal va'chomer* from a Canaanite maidservant. Read as bi'ah without chuppah, it proves *nisu'in*; Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak deflects it; Ravina rereads the whole exchange as a rabbinic question about *simfon*.

children.title: The Message to Netzivin and the Kal Va'chomer from a Maidservant
children.gist: R. Yehuda ben Beteira argues that betrothal money should permit terumah as a maidservant's purchase money does, yet concedes the Sages' rabbinic ban until chuppah.

bullets.text: Yochanan ben Bag Bag to R. Yehuda ben Beteira in Netzivin: I heard you say that a non-kohen's daughter betrothed to a kohen (*arusah bat Yisrael*) eats terumah.
R. Yehuda ben Beteira replies: and don't you say so? I know you are expert in the inner chambers of Torah; can't you draw a *kal va'chomer*?

The *kal va'chomer*: a Canaanite maidservant's bi'ah with a kohen doesn't permit her terumah, yet her purchase money does. A betrothed woman's bi'ah does permit terumah, so surely her betrothal money should.
"But what can I do": the Sages ruled that she may not eat terumah until she enters the chuppah, by rabbinic law.
Why does a logical inference need expertise? One must know the whole system to judge where a *kal va'chomer* can apply and what might undercut it.

children.title: Which Comparison? Bi'ah Without Chuppah Would Prove Nisu'in
children.gist: With chuppah on both sides there is no question, and chuppah on one side only is unfair; so the comparison must be bi'ah without chuppah, which makes sense only if bi'ah effects *nisu'in*.

bullets.text: If he compares bi'ah followed by chuppah with money followed by chuppah, she is fully married in both and eats terumah even by rabbinic law.
If bi'ah with chuppah vs. money without chuppah, the inference fails: one side has two stages and the other only one.
So he must mean bi'ah without chuppah vs. money without chuppah.

That works if bi'ah itself effects *nisu'in*: then it is obviously stronger than money. If bi'ah is only *erusin*, why would it be obvious for bi'ah and need a *kal va'chomer* for money? In both she is only betrothed.

children.title: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: Bi'ah With Chuppah, Money Without
children.gist: The *kal va'chomer* survives the two-stages objection when framed around chuppah; Ulla's reason explains the ban, and ben Bag Bag rejects the comparison because a maidservant's purchase is complete.

bullets.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: he does mean bi'ah with chuppah vs. money without it, and the *kal va'chomer* still holds.

Reframed: a maidservant's bi'ah doesn't permit terumah even with chuppah, yet her money does without chuppah. A betrothed woman's bi'ah permits terumah with chuppah, so her money should without chuppah.
The Sages' ban until chuppah is for Ulla's reason: while in her father's house she may feed terumah to her siblings and family.
Ben Bag Bag's rejection: in buying a maidservant nothing of the acquisition is left undone; in betrothal part of it, the marriage, is still outstanding.
The argument assumes money plays the same role in buying a slave and in betrothal; but acquiring a slave is one stage and marriage two, so the roles differ.

children.title: Ravina: The Question Was Simfon, Not Terumah by Torah Law
children.gist: Ravina recasts the exchange as a rabbinic dispute over *simfon*; ben Bag Bag explains why a slave purchase has no *simfon*, and the Gemara asks what then separates the two sages.

children.title: Ravina's Reading: Eat Terumah Without Fear of Simfon?
children.gist: By Torah law betrothal money plainly permits terumah; the message asked whether she may eat without worrying that a hidden blemish will void the betrothal.

bullets.text: Ravina: by Torah law it is obvious to Yochanan ben Bag Bag that money alone permits her terumah; his question concerned rabbinic law.
The message: I heard you say she eats terumah and we don't fear *simfon*, that he may find a blemish and the betrothal prove void retroactively, so that she ate terumah unlawfully.
The *kal va'chomer*: a maidservant's purchase money permits terumah with no fear of *simfon*; surely betrothal money should, before chuppah, with no such fear.
And again: the Sages forbade it until chuppah, for Ulla's reason, lest she feed her family.
Rashi: *simfon* is anything that cancels a transaction. Here the concern is *kiddushei ta'ut*, a betrothal made in error; the shiur notes how central such claims are in today's *agunah* discussions.

children.title: No Simfon in Buying a Slave: Exposed, Hidden, Thief, Bandit
children.gist: Ben Bag Bag rejects the *kal va'chomer* because a slave sale is never voided: every kind of blemish was either seen, irrelevant, to be expected, or public knowledge.

bullets.text: Ben Bag Bag holds there is no *simfon* in buying slaves. An exposed blemish: the master saw it and bought him anyway.
A hidden blemish: it makes no difference, since he wants the slave only for labor.
Even a thief or a gambler (*kuvyustus*): the sale stands, since such behavior is common among slaves and the buyer should have expected it.
An armed bandit sought or condemned by the government: such matters are publicized, so he took the risk.
The shiur asks whether a petty or compulsive thief fits this reasoning: such a trait is not public knowledge, so it might yet count as a blemish.

children.title: Both Forbid Her Terumah: So What Do They Dispute?
children.gist: Since both sages agree that by rabbinic decree she may not eat terumah before chuppah, the Gemara asks what practical difference remains between them.

bullets.text: The Gemara asks: according to both Yochanan ben Bag Bag and R. Yehuda ben Beteira, a betrothed non-kohen's daughter may not eat terumah by rabbinic decree. What, then, is the difference between them?

returns_to.note: Back to the rabbinic ban both sages accepted

children.continues: Continues on 11a with the Gemara's answer: what practical difference separates the two sages.

key_terms.definition: One of the three ways of effecting kiddushin: the man has intercourse with the woman for the purpose of betrothal, with her consent and before witnesses.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The daf asks which verse teaches it, which moment of the act acquires, and whether it effects full marriage at once.

key_terms.sense: a betrothed young woman who is a virgin
key_terms.definition: A young woman who is betrothed but not yet married and is still a virgin. One who has intercourse with her is liable to stoning, rather than the strangulation that applies to a married woman.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The baraita of ten men with a na'arah me'orasah tests whether only a husband renders her a non-virgin through atypical intercourse.

key_terms.sense: betrothal that can lead to permitted intercourse
key_terms.definition: The principle that a betrothal is valid only if intercourse between the couple would be permitted; betrothal that cannot lead to permitted intercourse does not take effect.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rava learns it from the word u'be'alah; the shiur contrasts Rashi, who applies it to the arayot, with Tosafot, who apply it to a prohibition the betrothal itself creates.

key_terms.sense: completion of the act of intercourse
key_terms.definition: The completion of intercourse, as opposed to its initial stage (ha'ara'ah). Laws that depend on intercourse can differ as to which stage is decisive.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Ameimar in the name of Rava rules that a man intends the completion, so kiddushei bi'ah takes effect at the end of the act.

key_terms.definition: The first stage of Jewish marriage, effected by kiddushin: the woman is forbidden to other men, but she does not yet live with her husband, and many of the marital rights and obligations do not yet apply.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Gemara asks whether kiddushei bi'ah creates only erusin, as money and document do, and tests the question against three sources.

key_terms.sense: the second stage of marriage (full marriage)
key_terms.definition: The second stage of Jewish marriage, usually effected by chuppah, after which the couple are fully married: the husband inherits his wife, a kohen becomes impure for her burial, and he alone annuls her vows.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The question is whether bi'ah effects nisu'in in one act; the reading of R. Yehuda ben Beteira's kal va'chomer as bi'ah without chuppah would prove that it does.

key_terms.sense: a factor that retroactively annuls a transaction
key_terms.definition: A defect discovered after a transaction that voids it retroactively, such as a hidden blemish that makes a betrothal one made in error.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Ravina reads the dispute over a betrothed woman eating terumah as a question of simfon; ben Bag Bag holds a slave purchase is never voided by simfon.

judgment_calls: The Ben Bag Bag exchange (10b.4–11a.5) is nested under the question of whether bi'ah effects nisu'in, since the Gemara introduces it as a 'come and hear' for that question. It could be a top-level section in its own right, given how far it moves into terumah and simfon.
Ravina's simfon reading and ben Bag Bag's slave-blemish reasoning are nested under the Ben Bag Bag section rather than set as a separate top-level topic, because they reinterpret the same exchange.

Rava's kiddushin ha'mesurin le'vi'ah, with the shiur's Rashi/Tosafot and Yom Kippur discussion, is kept as one child of the verse-derivations section rather than its own top-level section, since in the Gemara it answers how Rava uses u'be'alah.
The ten-men baraita (9b.21) and R. Zeira (10a.1–2) are grouped under one parent on Rebbi's be'ulat ba'al, as challenge and answer; they could have been siblings at the level of the verse derivations.
The shiur's Rambam/Ra'avad discussion of the fine is placed with R. Zeira's statement on the fine (10a.1), where it bears on the text, although the lecture takes it up at the end.
Tosafot's four reconciliations are placed only with techilat/sof bi'ah (10a.4–5), though the essay presents them twice.
coverage_notes: 9b.17–9b.21 was covered at the end of the previous shiur and at the start of this one; used that material and did not flag it.
The essay names the tanna of the 'both of them' baraita R. Yoshiyah; the text has R. Oshaya. Followed the text.
The essay calls Abaye's source a baraita; the text cites a Mishnah (Ketubot 46b). Followed the text.
The essay attributes 'I know you are expert in the chambers of Torah... a kal va'chomer' to ben Bag Bag; in the text it is R. Yehuda ben Beteira's reply. Followed the text.
The essay presents the 'what are the circumstances' analysis (10b.6–8) as ben Bag Bag's refutation; in the text it is the Gemara's own analysis. Followed the text.
The essay says Torah-law permission was obvious 'to Ravina'; the text has Ravina saying it was obvious to Yochanan ben Bag Bag. Followed the text.
The essay renders kuvyustus as kidnapper or violent criminal; the text has gambler. Followed the text.
The essay concludes that the discussion shows no need to read bi'ah as nisu'in; the text gives no such conclusion within this range. Left it out.
The essay explains Rebbi's first-rapist ruling as his being 'in the husband's position'; the Gemara grounds it in levado. Gave the Gemara's reason only.
The essay places the Ben Bag Bag exchange inside its techilat bi'ah discussion; followed the text's order.
The text of line 11a.5 was not provided; the last section ends there without stating its content.
The shiur's remarks on the Rambam/Ra'avad and the Tosafot Rid are placed at 10a.1 though given at the end of the lecture.
